newsitem.title: RWANDA: Shooting crackles in eastern Zairean city of Goma.
newsitem.headline: Shooting crackles in eastern Zairean city of Goma.

text.p: Gunfire crackled through the Zairean city of Goma on Sunday and foreign aid workers feared for more than a million people abandoned in east Zaire's war zone.
Sporadic gunfire in Goma city centre and around its airport, five km (three miles) to the north, could be heard in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi overnight and on Sunday morning.

But troops of the Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) turned away journalists trying to reach Goma from Gisenyi and Rwanda played down RPA intervention in fighting for the city pitting Zairean troops and exiled Rwandan Hutu militiamen against Tutsi rebels.

"We have categorically no intention of formally, militarily going in to Zaire. I don't believe anybody from the RPA is going there," said Rwandan Defence Ministry spokesman Emmanuel Ndahiro in Gisenyi.
"I am having discussions with (Rwandan) military authorities in Gisenyi and if we discover they were RPA (in Goma) we will treat them as individual, undisciplined cases," he told Reuters.

Witnesses however said RPA troops thrust into Goma by boat across Lake Kivu and by land on Friday. RPA reinforcements took Reuters journalists with them into Goma on Saturday and fought Zairean troops, who had lost control over much of the city.
More than a million refugees in eastern Rwanda were left to their fate on Saturday with the evacuation by road of more than 100 international aid workers from Goma after a string of rebel victories.

International efforts to help them were largely on hold on Sunday with aid agencies trying to contact the rebels to allow staff into rebel-held areas of eastern Zaire and very little news filtering out from the war zone on refugee movements.
Aid officials say they fear tens of thousands may die of hunger and disease in the war zone unless help reaches them.

Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said aid officials were worried a disaster was imminent on a scale similar to the deaths of 50,000 Rwandan refugees from mainly dysentery and cholera in Zaire in 1994.
He said thousands of local aid workers remained in the area but could not use vehicles because they might be looted and had no back up from agencies to monitor needs and direct aid.

He said there were probably more than 400,000 refugees crammed into Mugunga camp, just west of Goma and the largest refugee camp into the world, and more than 300,000 were either still on the road or in their camps in North Kivu province.
"There are half-a-million in the Bukavu and Uvira areas of Zaire unaccounted for," said Kessler, adding sanitation in Mugunga camp was very bad because of the crush of arrivals.
"A serious outbreak of a serious infectious disease could take place and none of us could do a thing," Dr John Howarth, medical director of the British agency Merlin, told Reuters.
"With the security situation as it is any humanitarian assessment could take weeks...by that time these people could be dying and until we are allowed access all this could go unobserved," he added.
Tens of thousands of Zaireans caught up in the fighting have joined refugees in the conflict zone. Some 200,000 Burundian Hutus who fled civil war at home are also in eastern Zaire.

Ndahiro said the Rwandan military could control Goma by firing from neighbouring Gisenyi and accused the international community of putting Rwanda in the dock when they should be paying more attention to those carrying out genocide in Zaire.

Rwanda's Tutsi-led army says Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen among the 1.1 million Hutu refugees who fled into Zaire during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda are conducting a similar campaign against ethnic Tutsis with Zairean backing.

It says the Rwandan troops and militiamen are fighting alongside Zaire's ragged army against the ethnic Tutsi Zairean rebels. Zaire accuses the armies of Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of invading, a charge they deny.
Zaire's government, which last month ordered Tutsis out of its South Kivu province, followed its army's rout in the past two weeks by on Saturday saying all refugees should be expelled.
Ndahiro said he was in Gisenyi to set up communications between the rebels in eastern Zaire and the Rwandan government.

From Brussels, a Rwandan Hutu lobby group -- the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy to Rwanda (RDR) -- said on Sunday only international military intervention could head off a humanitarian catastrophe in the Rwandan refugee camps in Zaire.
It said Rwanda's authorities were close to achieving their plan of chasing all aid workers out of the camps and leaving the refugees isolated so they could be wiped out without witnesses.
Tanzania state radio said on Sunday 1,700 refugees including 10 with gunshot wounds from Zaire had arrived in the western Tanzanian port of Kigoma after crossing Lake Tanganyika by boat.
International diplomatic efforts to find a solution have made little headway. A regional African summit is scheduled to be held in Kenya on Tuesday but Zaire says it will not attend.
